content: 1. According to ISO specifications, nozzles are color-coded to indicate their flow rate at a specific pressure. For example, the 8002E nozzle is yellow. 2. Space spray applications of insecticides are used for controlling vectors and public health pests. These applications can be performed using various equipment, such as hand-held thermal foggers with oil-based formulations, knapsack cold foggers, truck-mounted cold foggers, and vehicle-mounted thermal foggers. 3. Space treatments can also be applied inside aircraft cabins using aerosol cans. Additionally, space treatments can be conducted from aircraft to target disease vectors. 4. Space treatments are effective only against flying adult insects, such as mosquitoes, but do not affect larvae or pupae. These treatments have no residual activity due to the low dose used. 5. When conducting outdoor space treatments, it is essential to perform sequential treatments in the same area to control newly emerging adult mosquitoes before they can lay eggs. A minimum of three successive treatments should be applied at intervals not exceeding seven days. 6. For dengue vector control, treatments are best conducted in the early morning (after sunrise) and early evening (just before sunset) to avoid non-target insect pollinators. 7. Using insecticides with irritant effects that stimulate resting mosquitoes to fly can enhance the effectiveness of space treatments. 8. Timing treatments to avoid daylight hours minimizes the impact on non-target insect pollinators. 9. Space treatments using oil-based or water-based insecticidal products targeting adult mosquitoes are most effective when applied over a large area. This reduces the impact of mosquitoes emerging from pupae outside the treated area and entering the treated zone. 10. Effective space treatments may require integrating vehicle-mounted and manually carried spray equipment to cover areas not exposed to roadside fogging. 11. Proper mixing of insecticides, such as glycol, according to label instructions, is necessary to optimize the droplet spectrum. 12. Space treatments can also affect male mosquitoes, potentially disrupting mating. 13. Outdoor space treatments may not penetrate indoor areas, necessitating separate indoor space treatments using hand-held foggers. 14. Mosquito larvae and pupae inhabit diverse aquatic habitats, including small water storage containers, ponds, rivers, rice paddies, and drains. 15. Larval control involves applying various insecticide formulations, such as liquid sprays, granules, tablets, briquettes, and matrix-release products, depending on the habitat type, area size, and vegetation cover. 16. Larvicides can be applied using different types of sprayers, including compression, lever-operated, electric-powered knapsack sprayers, motorized mist blowers, or granule applicators for spot or broadcast treatments. 17. Thermal fogging with larger water-based droplets can be used to treat larval breeding areas. 18. Ultra-low volume (ULV) spray applications with motorized mist blowers or truck-mounted foggers can be used for area-wide larvicide applications in wetlands or around dwellings. 19. Care must be taken to ensure the correct dosage of larvicides is applied, and the products used must be suitable for treating water, especially drinking water for humans or animals. 20. Monitoring before and after treatment is necessary to locate breeding sites initially and assess the impact of larval control interventions in treated areas. 21. Vegetation near houses, especially around latrines, can be sprayed with residual insecticides to kill adult mosquitoes resting in the vegetation before entering homes. 22. Residual sprays are best applied using motorized mist blowers to project spray droplets into tree canopies and bushes where mosquitoes may rest. 23. Specifications for pesticide application equipment should include characteristics relevant to operator safety, robustness, and operational performance. 24. Equipment must be resistant to corrosion and chemical formulations, ensuring durability and proper functioning during normal use. 25. Spray tanks should be designed for complete drainage and marked with permanent graduations for accurate filling. 26. Equipment should include user manuals detailing operation, calibration, safety precautions, maintenance, and spare parts. 27. Straps on manually carried equipment should be wide enough to avoid discomfort and adjustable for proper fit. 28. Hoses must withstand twice the maximum recommended working pressure and should not kink, ensuring free flow. 29. Droplet spectrum requirements depend on the type of spray needed. For space treatments, droplets should be less than 30 µm in diameter to remain airborne longer, ideally in the 10–15 µm range for most vector species. 30. When applying larvicides to water surfaces, the median droplet size of aqueous sprays should be larger than 200 µm to ensure rapid fallout unless vegetation is present, in which case granules are recommended.
